intro: Twenty-five words is about one long sentence or two short ones. If you can explain an idea in that space, you understand it. Type your answer, then check it against the three things a complete answer needs.

items.q: Athens had a democracy about 2,500 years ago. Explain how Australia's democracy is different from it.
must: In Athens citizens voted directly on decisions
In Australia citizens elect representatives to make decisions for them
Only free Athenian men could take part; in Australia every adult citizen can vote
items.model: Athenians voted directly on decisions, but only free men could. Australians elect representatives to make laws for them, and every adult citizen can vote.

items.q: Explain what a representative democracy is, and name one thing citizens can still do between elections.
must: Citizens elect representatives
The representatives make laws and decisions on citizens' behalf
Between elections citizens can contact their MP, sign a petition, campaign or protest
items.model: Citizens elect members of Parliament to make laws and decisions for them. Between elections they can still write to their MP, sign petitions or campaign.

items.q: Explain how a referendum is different from an election.
must: An election chooses representatives
A referendum is a vote on changing the Constitution
A referendum passes only with a double majority
items.model: An election chooses our representatives. A referendum asks voters to change the Constitution, and passes only with a national majority plus a majority of states.

items.q: What is the double majority, and why does it make the Constitution hard to change?
must: A majority of voters across the whole country
A majority of voters in at least four of the six states
Both are needed at once, so a popular Yes can still fail
items.model: A referendum needs Yes from most voters nationally and from most voters in at least four states. Getting both at once is rare, so changes are uncommon.

items.q: Explain what the Constitution does. Include when it began.
must: It sets out how Australia is governed
It divides power between the federal and state governments and sets up Parliament
It came into effect on 1 January 1901, when the colonies federated
items.model: The Constitution is the rulebook for governing Australia. Since 1 January 1901 it has set up Parliament and divided power between the federal and state governments.

items.q: Explain the rule of law and why it matters in a democracy.
must: Everyone must follow the law, including leaders and law-makers
Independent courts apply the law to everyone equally
It stops people in power abusing that power
items.model: The rule of law means everyone, including the Prime Minister, must obey the law. Independent courts apply it equally, so power cannot be abused.

items.q: Explain why Australia has three levels of government, and give one responsibility of each level.
must: Dividing power puts decisions close to the people they affect
Federal: national matters such as defence, immigration or currency; state: schools, hospitals, police or roads
Local council: local services such as parks, libraries or local roads
items.model: Dividing power keeps decisions close to the people affected. The federal government handles defence and immigration, states run schools and hospitals, councils look after parks.

items.q: What is a federal system? Explain what happens when a state law and a federal law disagree.
must: Law-making power is divided between a national government and state or territory governments
Each level makes laws in its own areas
Where both can make laws and they clash, the federal law applies
items.model: In a federal system law-making power is shared between the national and state governments. Where both may make laws and they clash, the federal law applies.

items.q: Explain the separation of powers using the three branches, and say what could go wrong without it.
must: The legislature (Parliament) makes laws
The executive (Prime Minister, ministers, departments) puts laws into action
The judiciary (courts) interprets and applies laws; without the split, one group could hold all the power
items.model: Parliament makes laws, the executive carries them out and the courts interpret them. Splitting the roles stops any one group from holding all the power.

items.q: Why must judges be independent of the government? Explain.
must: Judges decide cases without pressure from Parliament or ministers
Courts can then rule against the government when it breaks the law
This protects people's rights and the rule of law
items.model: Independent judges decide cases on the law, not on what ministers want. That lets courts rule against the government and protects everyone's rights.

items.q: Explain how a bill becomes a law in the federal Parliament.
must: It is passed by the House of Representatives
It is passed by the Senate, which can amend or reject it
The Governor-General gives royal assent
items.model: A bill must pass the House of Representatives, then the Senate, which can amend or reject it. The Governor-General's royal assent then makes it law.

items.q: Explain what government accountability means, and give one way a government is held to account.
must: A government must explain and justify its decisions
It can be questioned, for example in Parliament, by journalists or by voters
It can be held responsible, for example by being voted out
items.model: Accountability means a government must explain its decisions and answer for them. Question time in Parliament, a free press and elections all hold it to account.

items.q: Explain the difference between a political party and a policy, with an example.
must: A party is an organised group sharing ideas about how Australia should be governed
A policy is a plan for dealing with a particular issue
An example of a policy, such as free school lunches or cheaper childcare
items.model: A political party is an organised group that shares ideas about governing Australia. A policy is one of its plans, such as making school lunches free.

items.q: Explain how a party forms government after a federal election.
must: Government is formed in the House of Representatives
It needs the support of more than half the members, 76 of 150
The leader of that party or coalition becomes Prime Minister
items.model: The party or coalition with more than half the House of Representatives, 76 of 150 seats, forms government, and its leader becomes Prime Minister.

items.q: What is a hung parliament, and what are two ways it can be resolved?
must: No party or coalition has a majority (76 seats)
Parties can agree to form a coalition
The largest party can govern as a minority with crossbench support
items.model: A hung parliament means nobody holds 76 seats. Parties may agree a coalition, or the largest party governs in minority with crossbench members' support.

items.q: Explain the difference between the Opposition and the crossbench.
must: The Opposition is the largest party or coalition not in government
The crossbench is made up of members of neither the government nor the Opposition: minor parties and independents
Both question the government and vote on bills
items.model: The Opposition is the biggest party outside government and offers an alternative. The crossbench is everyone else: minor parties and independents belonging to neither side.

items.q: Explain the difference between citizenship and national identity.
must: Citizenship is formal legal membership, with rights and responsibilities
National identity is a sense of belonging shaped by values, culture and experience
A person can have one without the other, and people experience identity differently
items.model: Citizenship is legal membership of Australia, with rights and responsibilities. National identity is a personal sense of belonging, which people feel and express in different ways.

items.q: Give two rights and two responsibilities of Australian citizens, and explain why the responsibilities matter.
must: Rights such as voting, standing for Parliament, holding a passport
Responsibilities such as obeying the law, enrolling and voting, serving on a jury
Democracy depends on citizens taking part
items.model: Citizens may vote, stand for Parliament and hold a passport. They must obey the law, enrol and vote, and serve on juries, because democracy needs participation.

items.q: Explain two things that have shaped Australia's national identity.
must: First Nations peoples' history of at least 65,000 years and connection to Country
British colonisation from 1788, which brought British political and legal traditions
Migration, which created a multicultural society with shared democratic values
items.model: Australia's identity grew from 65,000 years of First Nations culture, British institutions brought after 1788, and waves of migration that made a multicultural nation.

items.q: Explain what civic action is, and describe two lawful ways a Year 8 student could take it.
must: Action by an individual or group to influence an issue or improve the community
Examples such as a petition, a letter to an MP or councillor, a campaign, a peaceful protest or volunteering
It should be aimed at whoever actually makes the decision
items.model: Civic action is anything people do to influence an issue or improve their community. A student could start a petition or write to their local councillor.

items.q: Name the five characteristics of an effective law, and explain one of them.
must: Known, clear and understood, enforceable, stable, reflects society's values
One characteristic explained, for example enforceable means authorities can detect a breach and apply a consequence
Why that characteristic matters: people can follow the law and it is applied consistently
items.model: An effective law is known, clear, enforceable, stable and reflects society's values. Enforceable means police can tell when it is broken and apply a penalty.

items.q: Use the Victorian seatbelt law to explain how a law can be effective.
must: In 1970 Victoria became the first place in the world to make seatbelts compulsory
Road deaths fell, from 1,061 in 1970 to 923 in 1971
The law is clear and enforceable and now reflects society's values
items.model: Victoria's 1970 seatbelt law was clear and enforceable, deaths fell from 1,061 to 923 the next year, and most people now accept it as normal.

items.q: Explain the difference between a law and a rule.
must: A law is made and enforced by legal authorities such as Parliament, the courts and police
A rule is set by a group such as a school or club
Breaking a law has legal consequences; breaking a rule has consequences only within that group
items.model: A law is made by Parliament and enforced by police and courts, with legal penalties. A rule is set by a school or club and applies there.

items.q: Explain the three principles of justice.
must: Fairness: impartial processes, with each side given a fair chance to be heard
Equality: the law applies to everyone in the same way
Access: people can reach the legal system and make sense of it, whatever their money, language or location
items.model: Fairness means impartial decisions where each side is heard. Equality means the law treats everyone the same. Access means people can reach the system and make sense of it.

items.q: Explain the difference between equality and equity, with an example.
must: Equality is treating everyone the same
Equity is giving support according to need so everyone has a fair chance
An example, such as a ramp beside the stairs or large-print documents
items.model: Equality treats everyone the same, like one set of stairs for all. Equity gives extra support where needed, like a ramp, so everyone can actually get in.
